World.title: How an $8000 trip to Hamish and Andy’s New York pub exposes the Coalition’s retiree rort problem
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election How an $8000 trip to Hamish and Andy’s New York pub exposes the Coalition’s retiree rort problem Annika Smethurst July 15, 2026 — 7:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After Coalition MPs spent tens of thousands of taxpayer dollars on overseas trips on the eve of announcing their retirements from politics, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has vowed to drastically limit travel entitlements if elected. An analysis of domestic and international travel disclosures conducted by The Age found more than half-a-dozen Liberal and National Party MPs have collectively claimed more than $65,000 this term on interstate and overseas travel – including trips across North America, Europe and Asia – only to announce their retirements shortly after landing back in Victoria. Liberal MP Kim Wells in March. Darrian Traynor By contrast, the vast majority of state Labor MPs who have announced they will exit politics in November haven’t made any interstate or international travel claims during the past four years. In response, Wilson has pledged to treat taxpayer money “with respect” and rein in the perk by limiting the allowance to domestic travel, only if successful on election day.



“The international travel allowance is inconsistent with community expectations and if elected premier, I will scrap it,” Wilson told The Age. Former treasurer Kim Wells announced his retirement just five days after returning from a 12-night taxpayer-funded trip to New York and Hong Kong that cost Victorian taxpayers $8635. According to his travel report, Wells – who is currently a backbencher and the member for Rowville – said his reason for visiting the United States was to “investigate several areas relevant to my electorate business and work as a parliamentarian”. As part of the trip, Wells said he was keen to meet law and “enforcement decision makers” to discuss antisemitism and view the Hudson Yards.



“Plan to walk down to the High Line and Hudson Yards to familiarise myself with the area and to compare it with the former Melbourne Lord Mayor’s [Sally Capp’s] plan for the Greenline project,” Wells wrote in his travel report. But after landing in New York, his meeting with a representative from the Hudson Yards project “didn’t go ahead due to issues”. Old Mates Pub in Manhattan is among a number of Australian-owned businesses succeeding in New York. Alex Towle Wells had also planned to meet his former Liberal colleague, Sam Groth, at Old Mates Pub – a Manhattan bar partly owned by TV hosts Andy Lee and Hamish Blake – but was stood up by the former deputy Liberal leader. “We are keen to meet the owners and managers to get a first-hand brief on how New Yorkers view Victoria and Melbourne,” Wells wrote, before adding “meeting cancelled as Sam is unavailable”.



From New York, Wells flew to Hong Kong for four nights to meet with the Independent Commission Against Corruption. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Jess Wilson is trying to convince Victoria to trust her party, one High Street at a time On September 14, 2025, just five days after returning to Victoria, Wells announced his intention to quit at the November 2026 election. “After discussions with family, good mates, friends, branch members and supporters, I have decided not to contest the next election,” Wells wrote on his Facebook page. Under Wilson’s proposed changes, which will be introduced if she wins the election on November 28, Victorian MPs would still be able to use their allowance to travel domestically. Overseas ministerial travel, which is funded by government departments, would remain at the discretion of the premier.



Three sources speaking to The Age on the condition of confidentiality to discuss internal party matters said that more retiring Coalition MPs have taxpayer-funded trips planned for between now and November. However, one senior Liberal source, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters freely, said the policy had not gone to shadow cabinet or the party room and was unlikely to be supported. In August 2025, less than four months before his early exit from the Victorian parliament, Groth booked a trip to the US that cost taxpayers $11,153. However, he was forced to cancel last minute due to undergoing foot surgery. Parliament is currently seeking reimbursement for the amount from an insurance claim. The then member for Nepean’s disclosure said the trip included “parliamentary business meetings with key stakeholders” linked to his shadow portfolios of tourism, sport events and hospitality. In June 2025, former deputy Liberal leader David Hodgett also claimed taxpayer-funded interstate and overseas travel – six weeks before announcing his retirement on August 6.



The trips to Japan and Singapore were to “investigate research and explore political business and economic issues and opportunities as electorate business”, per Hodgett’s disclosure record, and cost Victorians more than $7000. Following his retirement announcement, Hodgett has continued to use taxpayer-funded travel entitlements for trips to Sydney in October 2025 ($1580), and Darwin in March ($2436) for what he described as “electorate and business meetings”. David Hodgett, the member for Croydon, will retire with the seat on a margin of just 1.18 per cent. Simon Schluter Liberal MP Bill Tilley has also continued to claim taxpayer-funded trips since his announcement in 2024 that he would retire at the November election. Last year, the member for Benambra claimed almost $10,000 to join Hodgett on his Japan trip. Tilley also billed taxpayers almost $2660 last July for return flights to Queensland to “undertake research, attending meetings, and carrying out administrative activities connected with boating and fishing”, as well as a two-day trip to Darwin for $4300.



Related Article Victorian election ‘We are not banjo-playing dimwits’: The deep rural resentment that will shape the election In January, Upper House Liberal MP Wendy Lovell travelled to Barbados for a conference held by the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, where she delivered a presentation on accessibility improvements to Parliament House. “Many of the MPs present at the session approached me during the conference to say how much they enjoyed my presentation. I also received feedback from one of the participants about disability access to our building,” Lovell noted in her post-travel report. “The MP who spoke to me pointed out that even the sign, to say disability access is via the side entry, is positioned at the top of the steps rather than at street level, and I have passed this feedback onto the deputy clerk of the Legislative Council,” she wrote. The 10-night trip cost taxpayers $11,410 and came three months before her exit from politics was announced. The clerk of the Parliament of Victoria, Bridget Noonan, as well as Labor MP Dylan Wight, also attended the conference.



Just weeks before he announced his decision to stand down as the member for East Gippsland, Nationals MP Tim Bull travelled to France and Belgium, with his allowance disclosure stating the trip was undertaken to visit every known grave on the Western Front of soldiers from his electorate. His international airfare claim totalled $1932. Related Article Victorian election ‘She scrolls’: The trick to Jess Wilson’s low-budget social media ploy Upper House MP Joe McCracken also claimed more than $900 to travel to Queensland to meet “with Queensland MP’s and government officials” in July last year. Six months later, he announced he would not recontest his seat. In its current form, the allowances scheme reimburses MPs for travel undertaken as part of their parliamentary or electorate duties, but contains no separate rules for members who have decided to retire. Parliamentary disclosures show six retiring Labor MPs – Jackson Taylor, Steve McGhie, Jordan Crugnale, Mary-Anne Thomas, Gayle Tierney and Natalie Hutchins – made no interstate or international parliamentary travel claims in the years leading up to their retirements.



Outgoing Nationals MP Peter Walsh, Greens MP Tim Read, and former Liberal leader Michael O’Brien also made no interstate or overseas parliamentary travel claims before or after announcing they would quit politics at the next election. World.title: How China’s EV boom spun dangerously out of control
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesElectric vehicles Opinion How China’s EV boom spun dangerously out of control

Juliana Liu July 15, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

China’s electric vehicle industry is often held up as proof that the central government successfully engineered global champions through massive subsidies. But for the likes of dominant players BYD, Zhejiang Geely Holding Group and Chery Automobile, breakthroughs came after years of decentralised experimentation and ferocious competition. That process created a fragmented market plagued by too many players producing too many cars — a problem that will be difficult to resolve. Nowhere is this more apparent than in Beijing’s relationship with Brussels. A year after winning a tariff war with the US, China is on the cusp of a similar conflict with the European Union. There are now more than 140 brands in China making clean-energy cars, including battery electric vehicles and hybrids. Bloomberg Efforts to offset a sluggish domestic market with overseas growth is a major source of tension. The EU’s trade deficit with China has reached more than $US1 billion ($1.5 billion) a day, sparking worries about long-term industrial decline. Chinese models overtook sales of Japanese vehicles there for the first time in May, despite tariffs imposed by the bloc two years ago. EU and Chinese officials have given themselves until October to produce a joint plan to tackle the imbalance. Understanding how the industry got to this point explains why there are no easy solutions. The first thing to recognise is that the central authorities in China never intended to incubate so many carmakers. There are now more than 140 brands making clean-energy cars, including battery electric vehicles and hybrids, according to consulting firm AlixPartners.



A study published in this month’s edition of The China Journal, an academic publication, challenges the prevailing idea that top-down industrial policy was the primary driver of China’s EV boom. The 1980s reform period onwards favoured large state-owned automakers, noted co-authors Fengming Lu and Xiao Ma. There were nine designated firms, including China FAW Group and SAIC Motor Corp. They were showered with preferential treatment, including state credit, subsidised loans and the pick of partners when foreign vehicle makers arrived eager to form joint ventures in exchange for access to the emerging market. Related Article Electric vehicles How the arrival of a BYD ship marks a sea change in Australian motoring Even though Beijing tightly restricted new entrants, regional governments motivated by the prospect of jobs, tax revenue and bragging rights began to behave more like corporations. They became active investors, promoters or, in some cases, owners of local enterprises. This approach, while attractive to regional governments, ended up creating a capacity glut that is weighing on the earnings of many global carmakers. Mercedes-Benz said last week that intense competition contributed to an 8 per cent decline in second-quarter deliveries. BMW slashed its profit outlook in June and Volkswagen’s executives are reportedly worried about long-term survival. Many of today’s top EV companies emerged because local governments circumvented the rules by partnering with private companies. Their scrappy underdog status made them more nimble than state-owned counterparts, helping them to eventually dominate the industry.



Chery, China’s largest exporter, came into existence after the city of Wuhu in the south-eastern province of Anhui sold a cement business and decided to launch a carmaker. Geely, which vies with BYD as the top EV seller, was backed by the wealthy provincial government of Zhejiang. Shenzhen-based BYD worked with a number of cities as it expanded. Chery, China’s largest exporter, came into existence after the city of Wuhu in the south-eastern province of Anhui sold a cement business and decided to launch a carmaker. AP The bottom-up model produced some of China’s most successful companies. But it also encouraged local officials to back as many contenders as possible, creating excess capacity. Even though the property downturn that began five years ago left regional governments with less revenue from land sales, they arguably now have an even greater incentive to develop industries that can replenish their coffers. This could explain why the number of automakers selling new-energy cars has not substantially declined, even as margins and profitability have fallen due to greater competition. Last year, 23 new brands entered the industry, while only nine exited. Consolidation may make economic sense, but it often runs counter to political incentives. Local governments remain reluctant to let hometown stalwarts fail because they provide potential job growth during an economic downturn. That’s an uncomfortable reality for Beijing and its trade partners.

World.title: Winmar ‘devastated’ by AFL hall of fame eviction, plans to appeal assault conviction
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Winmar ‘devastated’ by AFL hall of fame eviction, plans to appeal assault conviction Andrew Wu Updated July 15, 2026 — 9:10pm ,first published 1:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former AFL star Nicky Winmar has been expelled from the Australian Football Hall of Fame despite his iconic stand to stamp out racism in the game. The AFL Commission revoked his membership after the former St Kilda champion’s recent conviction for assaulting a woman, while the Saints have suspended the club great from their Hall of Fame. Former AFL player Nicky Winmar outside court. AAP Winmar, 60, told News Corp that he planned to appeal against the conviction and was “devastated and extremely upset” by the league’s move. The commission has the power to remove an inductee through amendments made to the Hall of Fame’s charter in 2023.



It can remove an inductee “if they have been charged with or found guilty of an indictable offence and/or if the inductee engages in conduct which the commission considers is prejudicial to the interests of the AFL or is conduct which brings the AFL, the inductee, or Australian Football into disrepute”. Winmar was inducted into the Australian Football Hall of Fame in 2022. AFL Photos via Getty Images The AFL has not used this power to remove North Melbourne great Wayne Carey, who was inducted into the Australian Football Hall of Fame in 2010 despite having been convicted of assaulting a female police officer in the US in 2007. That occurred after his then girlfriend Kate Neilson accused him of smashing a wine glass against her face. She did not press charges. He pleaded guilty to indecent assault after grabbing a woman’s breast in 1995. The AFL blocked Carey from being inducted as a legend in the NSW Australian Football Hall of Fame in 2024 at a time when the league was taking a stance honouring victims of violence against women.



Winmar hit back at what he claimed were double standards by the AFL. “Again, I am appealing the verdict, and would also like some clarity from the AFL as to why there are other players in the Australian Football Hall of Fame who have been found guilty of similar charges, and why I have been removed before the appeal has even been heard,” he told News Corp. Carey’s offending happened before he was inducted and before the changes to the Hall of Fame charter in 2023, and the AFL has not used the power retrospectively. The AFL removed football great Barry Cable from the Hall of Fame in 2023 and stripped him of his legend status after he was found in a civil trial to have sexually abused a Perth girl during his playing career. In a separate criminal trial relating to a different girl, Cable was found not guilty of historical child sex abuse charges dating back to the 1960s. Related Article Courts Statue of Nicky Winmar to be removed after he smashed woman’s head into a door



Cable was a two-time VFL premiership player with the North Melbourne Football Club in the 1970s. Winmar, 60, was found guilty of three counts of assaulting a woman in the Bendigo Magistrates’ Court earlier this month. Winmar declined to comment when contacted by this masthead on Wednesday. A dashing and highly skilled forward and wingman, Winmar played 251 games for the Saints and the Western Bulldogs. He was a key figure in the AFL’s fight against racism in the 1990s after famously lifting his jumper and pointing to his skin during a game against Collingwood at Victoria Park in 1993 in which he was racially abused by Magpies supporters.



The AFL acknowledged Winmar’s contribution to the game in a statement on Wednesday, explaining why one of the game’s highest individual accolades was taken off him. “The Australian Football Hall of Fame exists to recognise the highest achievements in our game and admission to it is one of the greatest honours Australian football can bestow,” AFL chairman Craig Drummond said. “The commission has a responsibility to protect the integrity and reputation of that honour. Related Article Courts Nicky Winmar’s statue removed from Optus Stadium after assault conviction



“Violence against women has no place. Not in our community, not in our game, and not in the values the Australian Football Hall of Fame seeks to uphold. “The commission acknowledges Nicky Winmar’s significant contribution to Australian football and his place in our history. However, the recent findings against him render inappropriate his place in the Australian Football Hall of Fame.” The Saints have not expelled Winmar from their Hall of Fame. “A determination regarding Winmar’s ongoing place in the Hall of Fame will be made following the formal conclusion of the full legal process, including the completion of any appeal,” the Saints said in a statement released minutes after the AFL’s. “Violence against women has no place in our community. Our thoughts are with anyone impacted by this matter.”



The WA government ordered that a statue of Winmar, recreating his famous stance against racism, be taken down from outside of Optus Stadium in Perth following his conviction. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Aced by an honorary Aussie
World.content:
“Like many, I was saddened to hear of the passing of Sam Neill,” says John Clarke of Lorn. “In the many tributes, however, I’ve not seen any reference to his outstanding performance in the series Reilly, Ace of Spies. It was extremely popular, and from memory, the single of the theme tune made it to the Top 40, which wasn’t bad for something based on a theme by Shostakovich. Vale Sam.” With that name, Granny was sure that John would endorse Death in Brunswick.

Keeping it reel, Alan Phillips of Mosman notes: “When I was a kid, we didn’t go to the movies or the pictures (C8), we went to the flicks.”

Andrew Lishmund of Castle Hill recalls the odd drawback regarding the University of NSW scavenger hunt (C8) in the 1970s: “A current subpoena to appear in court was devalued in the protest era – too easy to come by. A good ploy was to ‘kidnap’ an overseas performer and make them give a live show at the Roundhouse. One student was difficult to beat because elephants rated highly, and he turned up with a pair of them. He was a relative of the owner of a circus.”

“One 1950s Commemoration Day stunt that gained maximum points was when students from the sandstone edifice stormed a visiting US aircraft carrier,” writes Gillian Kendrigan of Evatt (ACT). “Dressed as pirates with cardboard cutlasses, a dawn raid gained them the bridge where one pirate pulled the Action Stations lever. About 2500 personnel jumped out of bed and dressed in their special actions uniforms before the order was countermanded five minutes later. Any C8-ers owning up?”

“In 1969, I was a 20-year-old ‘Nasho’ during the Vietnam War,” says Jim Rogers of Byron Bay. “When I was posted at Taskforce Headquarters, Moorebank, a colleague was the Brigadier’s batman and drove him around and looked after his limo. We were tasked with washing it and managed to apply a ‘Vietnam Moratorium Now’ sticker to the back bumper that wasn’t discovered for some time. The whole squad was put on punishment details but no one ratted!”

World.title: All tenants should be afforded their dignity
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters All tenants should be afforded their dignity July 15, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Georgie Armstrong’s account of living in an affordable apartment is heartbreaking (″⁣Hidden price of affordable housing″⁣, 15/7). After overcoming life events that could be just around the corner for any of us, she finally found the security of a home of her own that everyone deserves. It is disturbing that such an important government-backed program creates a new underclass. It might be reasonable that owners and tenants who pay more have access to particular services such as swimming pools, but it is important that all people living in mixed residential spaces retain their dignity as members of that community. The idea of a ″⁣poor door″⁣ is outrageous.

Judy Williams, Beaumaris This distinction is a form of apartheid

It is disgraceful for a Labor government to allow developers to get away with imposing a form of apartheid on residents of affordable housing units in otherwise standard apartment blocks. Thanks to Georgie Armstrong for exposing this. Thanks also to the regular resident who escorted Georgie into the restricted area so she could attend the weekly residents’ games night. The housing and/or planning minister should insist that tenants of affordable housing in Georgie’s block be immediately given the same access to the swimming pool, rooftop garden and barbecue facilities, along with the same quality of pictures on the walls, plants, benches and carpets.

They should also insist that affordable housing be scattered throughout future developments that receive concessions for providing a quota of affordable housing, not stigmatised on separate ″⁣affordable housing″⁣ floors.

And they should remember that many of us are only a job, a partner or a health crisis away from needing affordable housing, which should be provided by government as public housing, not left to the mercy of developers.

Rosemary West, Edithvale An entrance into ‘classism’

Anecdotally, many of us bemoan the widening gap between the ″⁣haves and have nots″⁣: now it’s being highlighted by separate entrances and restricted access to facilities in apartments. Georgie Armstrong describes her experience of being segregated in her apartment building – because she has access to affordable housing among her wealthier neighbours – as ″⁣humiliating″⁣.

While state governments are now emulating the US and UK trend of separating residents in apartment buildings according to their income status, international sociologists/demographers and even criminologists are reviewing the detrimental impact of this practice on low-income families being segregated. Of course, it festers resentment, as Armstrong describes the ″⁣classism″⁣ which makes her feel inferior.

In London, this segregation is now being revisited with Walthamstow MP Stella Creasy exclaiming: “Separate doors for rich and poor tenants is not the Walthamstow way – how could you design such a thing and think it acceptable?“

Indeed. Is seems it is now becoming ″⁣the Australian way″⁣ as governments, architects, developers adopt a process with scant regard for the sociological consequences.

Sally Davis, Malvern East



Segregation of tenants is unconscionable

Georgie Armstrong’s piece made me sick because it highlighted the truth about Jacinta Allan’s much-lauded public-private residential developments. How dare the government expose the public housing tenants to such segregation. To have limited access to facilities and have second-rate fitouts is unconscionable.

Based on Armstrong’s experience we, the smug middle class, should do what we can to stop the government’s decision to demolish Department of Housing’s high-rise buildings. I, for one, put dignity before development.

Chris Morgan, Northcote THE FORUM Justice for Isla

Supporters for Isla Bell were at the Supreme Court on Tuesday (″⁣Isla’s mum says prosecutors have failed victims of crime″⁣, 15/7). They would not have had to have been there if the Office of Public Prosecutions had done its job. As an ordinary citizen I would like it explained to me how the OPP actually makes decisions because I cannot see how this case has been allowed to transpire into a fiasco. There seems no thought given to Isla, a young woman in her prime. We put faith in our courts and juries to carry out justice.

I expect the law to do its job and treat Isla as a young woman, not a statistic, and let a jury decide. She did not kill herself and wrap herself in plastic and climb into a fridge. We want justice for her.

Nola Cormick, Albert Park Angry voices

On the steps of the Supreme Court on Tuesday, angry voices were heard urging the politicians of this country, especially men, to step up and change the legislation that currently favours perpetrators of femicide. Victims’ voices are not heard in court. The downgrading or dropping of charges deny the rights of victims and minimise the consequences for perpetrators.

The increasing number of women killed by men known to them is horrific and a statistic that should cause national embarrassment. Our legal system has denied these women justice. It is time for change. This story was front page news on The Age. It should be front page news every day.

Marie Spokes, Ascot Vale Change priorities

The aim of a royal commission is not to bring about culture change (“Allan digs in on Big Build inquiry”, 15/7). It is about bringing to light the decisions, processes and systems that led to a disaster. The sum of $15 billion of public money, plenty of it in the hands of criminals, deserves the highest level of investigation possible and accountabilities apportioned. Only then can culture changes be effected.

Tricia Bulic, Highton



Just doing business

Peter Bartlett (Comment, 15/7) argues that we should have a royal commission to once again rid the state and country of corruption in the building industry as exposed by The Age’s investigative journalists. It was successful in the past and Bartlett thinks it would be successful now in bringing those responsible to justice. He probably is right if it can follow the money trail right to the top.

I’m sure some union bosses and CEOs of construction companies and some politicians would be shuddering in their boots at the thought, but I’m not sure about the criminal bosses, who would see it as just part of the risk of doing business.

Paul Chivers, Box Hill North Enhancing reputation

Jacinta Allan’s decision not to hold a royal commission into the Big Build is intriguing. Indeed, as Sir Humphrey in Yes, Minister would say, it is courageous. The opposition say they will establish such a royal commission if they win government and they will set the terms of reference. If the Labor government set this up now, they would set the terms of reference and appoint the commissioners. The premier has pointed to the Dyson Heydon royal commission into unions as proof that such inquiries achieve very little. There are many other examples of royal commissions achieving much more, such as the one into robo-debt. Surely, Allan’s reputation would be enhanced if she decided to go ahead and call the royal commission now.

Pauline Brown, Woodend No justifying vandals

Reading columnist Shaun Hossack write on Melbourne’s graffiti vandals (Comment, 13/7) made me feel like I was living in a parallel universe. Somehow likening Rone and Adnate to the vandals on seemingly every flat surface in Melbourne (and virtually every lamp post in our city) seems to be drawing a very long bow. Hossack may think people come from across the globe to view our CBD laneways, but I have never seen busloads of tourists stopping on the Monash to photograph talentless taggers. It’s time we said enough is enough and start to take this illegal vandalism more seriously. Most people hate this blight on our city so let’s stop trying to justify it. And let’s begin by banning all spray cans now.

Neale Meagher, Malvern Smart investment needed

It is not surprising that our wages and productivity are declining in real terms (″⁣Australia’s real wages slump one of the worst in developed world″⁣, 10/7). We have been relying on rapid population growth to solve all our problems. It certainly ticks all the boxes for government and big business: increasing tax income, suppressing wages and increasing demand for goods and services, without having done anything to improve productivity, explore innovation, increase workforce participation, or improve education and training outcomes. Instead, more of our environmental assets are being trashed, inequality is super-charged and climate change ignored.

Our quality of life is deteriorating. Germany and most Nordic countries have superior GDP per capita with slow or declining population growth; sustainable investment in natural and human resources is critical if we are to have a future to look forward to.

Jennie Epstein, Little River It’s not entertainment

With some clubs now realising that ″⁣ticketed″⁣ matches are deterring fans from attending, they could attract more by ditching the US-style hoopla and confected ″⁣excitement″⁣ by ditching overly loud music, flashing lights, and announcers screeching into the microphone ″⁣make some noise″⁣. I know people who don’t go any more because of this ″⁣entertainment″⁣.

George Djoneff, Mitcham



The safer codes

Soccer and basketball each have many more participants in Australia than Australian rules football. With the number of dangerous tackles in AFL matches being cleared by the AFL tribunal in 2026, parents will decide the future of Australian rules.

John Hennessy, Montmorency No vision to see here

Further to your correspondent’s AFL metaphor of One Nation and Pauline Hanson (Letters, 14/7), Hanson has really taken on the dual role of captain-coach. That style of leadership went out of fashion at about the time when Australia embraced multiculturalism in all its richness and diversity in terms of religious observance, cuisine, language, fashion and, dare I say, soccer as the world game. Hanson’s nostalgic view of Australia is a haven for those who feel threatened by the Australia of today and want to drag it backwards. Where’s the vision in that?

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris There’s no comparison

Your correspondent (Letters, 14/7) suggested that Pauline Hanson was acting more like a grandmother than a politician.

I am a grandmother.

I acknowledge and respect the traditional owners of our land, say thank you for our multicultural society, believe that most workers do their best, support maternity leave and child care, am pro-choice, appreciate the solar panels supplying renewable power to my home and the electrical vehicle that takes me where I need to go. I make decisions based on science and facts and believe that climate change is real.

My values, shared with my children and grandchildren, are underpinned by the belief that we should treat others the way we want to be treated. I have also learnt that wealth does not guarantee happiness nor wisdom.

Please do not compare me to her.

Sophie Cuttriss, Inverloch Trump in dire straits

So if I understand this correctly, prior to the US and Israel striking Iran in February, the Strait of Hormuz was fully open to all shipping. No fees or charges were applied to shipping using it.

Once the war started one of Iran’s retaliatory acts was to close the Strait. In addition, they announced that they would impose a fee on ships transiting the Strait once the war was over.

Those advising US President Donald Trump warned him of this potential development prior to the US/Israel strikes in February. This advice was ignored.

Now, with the war continuing, Trump outlined his plan to open the Strait and impose a 20 per cent fee on ships using it. This fee would be imposed because the US is protecting the Strait for the rest of the world. He has now ditched that idea.

The great negotiator and “leader” of the free world proves once again he is truly a genius.

Jack Morris, Kennington Strange decision

Given our high consumption of berries for their health benefits, what possible reason could the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority have for allowing such potentially dangerous levels of a pesticide known to have adverse health effects (″⁣Experts slam plan for berry ‘forever’ chemicals″⁣, 15/7)?

Banning or significantly reducing the use of forever chemicals seems like a no-brainer.

Vikki O’Neill, Ashburton



Caught offside

I must disagree with your correspondents (Letters, 14/7 and 15/7). Barnaby Joyce should be ineligible to play as he is clearly offside.

Russell Kidd, Carnegie Good for a chat

For the federal government to work out what the proposed Office of AI should cover, I presume they will ask ChatGPT?

John Murray, Hawthorn East AND ANOTHER THING Victoria

I tend to agree with Jacinta Allan. From my observation, most royal commissions are time consuming, expensive, become a lawyers’ picnic and ultimately achieve very little.

Phil Alexander, Eltham Jacinta Allan, Victorians aren’t interested in your ″⁣new hospitals promotional tour″⁣. They’re worried about their living costs, repair of country roads and how you will pay down Labor’s near-$200 billion debt.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill



What’s wrong with Victorian government school teachers being the best paid in the country? It may still not be adequate but it would set a precedent (″⁣State school teachers vote to strike for 24 hours in pay row″⁣, 15/7).

Suzanne Palmer-Holton, Seaford Trump

Is this a new record for TACO? Twenty per cent shipping tariff in the Strait of Hormuz one day, zero the next. Way to go, Donald Trump.

Graham Fetherstonhaugh, North Fitzroy The Middle East is “hurtling back towards full-scale war” (″⁣Trump restarts blockade, flags toll″⁣, 15/7). Our long-term transport fuel security cries out for majority renewable energy, generated in Australia.

John Hughes, Mentone Furthermore

Many millions of people would not understand the meaning of the word trillion. Indeed few people can grasp the concept of a trillion dollars. Just think how it could make a billion people millionaires.

John Walsh, Watsonia Judging by the way they roll around in agony every time they fall over. Soccer players must feel pain a lot more than AFL players.

Ron Mather, Melbourne Finally

I would like to suggest some field work for archaeology students: dig down into the rubbish along our highways and use carbon dating to see how long it has been there.

Tony Blackshaw, Officer

World.title: How an $8000 trip to Hamish and Andy’s New York pub exposes the Coalition’s retiree rort problem
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election How an $8000 trip to Hamish and Andy’s New York pub exposes the Coalition’s retiree rort problem Annika Smethurst July 15, 2026 — 7:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After Coalition MPs spent tens of thousands of taxpayer dollars on overseas trips on the eve of announcing their retirements from politics, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has vowed to drastically limit travel entitlements if elected. An analysis of domestic and international travel disclosures conducted by The Age found more than half-a-dozen Liberal and National Party MPs have collectively claimed more than $65,000 this term on interstate and overseas travel – including trips across North America, Europe and Asia – only to announce their retirements shortly after landing back in Victoria. Liberal MP Kim Wells in March. Darrian Traynor By contrast, the vast majority of state Labor MPs who have announced they will exit politics in November haven’t made any interstate or international travel claims during the past four years. In response, Wilson has pledged to treat taxpayer money “with respect” and rein in the perk by limiting the allowance to domestic travel, only if successful on election day.



“The international travel allowance is inconsistent with community expectations and if elected premier, I will scrap it,” Wilson told The Age. Former treasurer Kim Wells announced his retirement just five days after returning from a 12-night taxpayer-funded trip to New York and Hong Kong that cost Victorian taxpayers $8635. According to his travel report, Wells – who is currently a backbencher and the member for Rowville – said his reason for visiting the United States was to “investigate several areas relevant to my electorate business and work as a parliamentarian”. As part of the trip, Wells said he was keen to meet law and “enforcement decision makers” to discuss antisemitism and view the Hudson Yards.



“Plan to walk down to the High Line and Hudson Yards to familiarise myself with the area and to compare it with the former Melbourne Lord Mayor’s [Sally Capp’s] plan for the Greenline project,” Wells wrote in his travel report. But after landing in New York, his meeting with a representative from the Hudson Yards project “didn’t go ahead due to issues”. Old Mates Pub in Manhattan is among a number of Australian-owned businesses succeeding in New York. Alex Towle Wells had also planned to meet his former Liberal colleague, Sam Groth, at Old Mates Pub – a Manhattan bar partly owned by TV hosts Andy Lee and Hamish Blake – but was stood up by the former deputy Liberal leader. “We are keen to meet the owners and managers to get a first-hand brief on how New Yorkers view Victoria and Melbourne,” Wells wrote, before adding “meeting cancelled as Sam is unavailable”.



From New York, Wells flew to Hong Kong for four nights to meet with the Independent Commission Against Corruption. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Jess Wilson is trying to convince Victoria to trust her party, one High Street at a time On September 14, 2025, just five days after returning to Victoria, Wells announced his intention to quit at the November 2026 election. “After discussions with family, good mates, friends, branch members and supporters, I have decided not to contest the next election,” Wells wrote on his Facebook page. Under Wilson’s proposed changes, which will be introduced if she wins the election on November 28, Victorian MPs would still be able to use their allowance to travel domestically. Overseas ministerial travel, which is funded by government departments, would remain at the discretion of the premier.



Three sources speaking to The Age on the condition of confidentiality to discuss internal party matters said that more retiring Coalition MPs have taxpayer-funded trips planned for between now and November. However, one senior Liberal source, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters freely, said the policy had not gone to shadow cabinet or the party room and was unlikely to be supported. In August 2025, less than four months before his early exit from the Victorian parliament, Groth booked a trip to the US that cost taxpayers $11,153. However, he was forced to cancel last minute due to undergoing foot surgery. Parliament is currently seeking reimbursement for the amount from an insurance claim. The then member for Nepean’s disclosure said the trip included “parliamentary business meetings with key stakeholders” linked to his shadow portfolios of tourism, sport events and hospitality. In June 2025, former deputy Liberal leader David Hodgett also claimed taxpayer-funded interstate and overseas travel – six weeks before announcing his retirement on August 6.



The trips to Japan and Singapore were to “investigate research and explore political business and economic issues and opportunities as electorate business”, per Hodgett’s disclosure record, and cost Victorians more than $7000. Following his retirement announcement, Hodgett has continued to use taxpayer-funded travel entitlements for trips to Sydney in October 2025 ($1580), and Darwin in March ($2436) for what he described as “electorate and business meetings”. David Hodgett, the member for Croydon, will retire with the seat on a margin of just 1.18 per cent. Simon Schluter Liberal MP Bill Tilley has also continued to claim taxpayer-funded trips since his announcement in 2024 that he would retire at the November election. Last year, the member for Benambra claimed almost $10,000 to join Hodgett on his Japan trip. Tilley also billed taxpayers almost $2660 last July for return flights to Queensland to “undertake research, attending meetings, and carrying out administrative activities connected with boating and fishing”, as well as a two-day trip to Darwin for $4300.



Related Article Victorian election ‘We are not banjo-playing dimwits’: The deep rural resentment that will shape the election In January, Upper House Liberal MP Wendy Lovell travelled to Barbados for a conference held by the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association, where she delivered a presentation on accessibility improvements to Parliament House. “Many of the MPs present at the session approached me during the conference to say how much they enjoyed my presentation. I also received feedback from one of the participants about disability access to our building,” Lovell noted in her post-travel report. “The MP who spoke to me pointed out that even the sign, to say disability access is via the side entry, is positioned at the top of the steps rather than at street level, and I have passed this feedback onto the deputy clerk of the Legislative Council,” she wrote. The 10-night trip cost taxpayers $11,410 and came three months before her exit from politics was announced. The clerk of the Parliament of Victoria, Bridget Noonan, as well as Labor MP Dylan Wight, also attended the conference.



Just weeks before he announced his decision to stand down as the member for East Gippsland, Nationals MP Tim Bull travelled to France and Belgium, with his allowance disclosure stating the trip was undertaken to visit every known grave on the Western Front of soldiers from his electorate. His international airfare claim totalled $1932. Related Article Victorian election ‘She scrolls’: The trick to Jess Wilson’s low-budget social media ploy Upper House MP Joe McCracken also claimed more than $900 to travel to Queensland to meet “with Queensland MP’s and government officials” in July last year. Six months later, he announced he would not recontest his seat. In its current form, the allowances scheme reimburses MPs for travel undertaken as part of their parliamentary or electorate duties, but contains no separate rules for members who have decided to retire. Parliamentary disclosures show six retiring Labor MPs – Jackson Taylor, Steve McGhie, Jordan Crugnale, Mary-Anne Thomas, Gayle Tierney and Natalie Hutchins – made no interstate or international parliamentary travel claims in the years leading up to their retirements.



Outgoing Nationals MP Peter Walsh, Greens MP Tim Read, and former Liberal leader Michael O’Brien also made no interstate or overseas parliamentary travel claims before or after announcing they would quit politics at the next election. World.title: How China’s EV boom spun dangerously out of control
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesElectric vehicles Opinion How China’s EV boom spun dangerously out of control

Juliana Liu July 15, 2026 — 7:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

China’s electric vehicle industry is often held up as proof that the central government successfully engineered global champions through massive subsidies. But for the likes of dominant players BYD, Zhejiang Geely Holding Group and Chery Automobile, breakthroughs came after years of decentralised experimentation and ferocious competition. That process created a fragmented market plagued by too many players producing too many cars — a problem that will be difficult to resolve. Nowhere is this more apparent than in Beijing’s relationship with Brussels. A year after winning a tariff war with the US, China is on the cusp of a similar conflict with the European Union. There are now more than 140 brands in China making clean-energy cars, including battery electric vehicles and hybrids. Bloomberg Efforts to offset a sluggish domestic market with overseas growth is a major source of tension. The EU’s trade deficit with China has reached more than $US1 billion ($1.5 billion) a day, sparking worries about long-term industrial decline. Chinese models overtook sales of Japanese vehicles there for the first time in May, despite tariffs imposed by the bloc two years ago. EU and Chinese officials have given themselves until October to produce a joint plan to tackle the imbalance. Understanding how the industry got to this point explains why there are no easy solutions. The first thing to recognise is that the central authorities in China never intended to incubate so many carmakers. There are now more than 140 brands making clean-energy cars, including battery electric vehicles and hybrids, according to consulting firm AlixPartners.



A study published in this month’s edition of The China Journal, an academic publication, challenges the prevailing idea that top-down industrial policy was the primary driver of China’s EV boom. The 1980s reform period onwards favoured large state-owned automakers, noted co-authors Fengming Lu and Xiao Ma. There were nine designated firms, including China FAW Group and SAIC Motor Corp. They were showered with preferential treatment, including state credit, subsidised loans and the pick of partners when foreign vehicle makers arrived eager to form joint ventures in exchange for access to the emerging market. Related Article Electric vehicles How the arrival of a BYD ship marks a sea change in Australian motoring Even though Beijing tightly restricted new entrants, regional governments motivated by the prospect of jobs, tax revenue and bragging rights began to behave more like corporations. They became active investors, promoters or, in some cases, owners of local enterprises. This approach, while attractive to regional governments, ended up creating a capacity glut that is weighing on the earnings of many global carmakers. Mercedes-Benz said last week that intense competition contributed to an 8 per cent decline in second-quarter deliveries. BMW slashed its profit outlook in June and Volkswagen’s executives are reportedly worried about long-term survival. Many of today’s top EV companies emerged because local governments circumvented the rules by partnering with private companies. Their scrappy underdog status made them more nimble than state-owned counterparts, helping them to eventually dominate the industry.



Chery, China’s largest exporter, came into existence after the city of Wuhu in the south-eastern province of Anhui sold a cement business and decided to launch a carmaker. Geely, which vies with BYD as the top EV seller, was backed by the wealthy provincial government of Zhejiang. Shenzhen-based BYD worked with a number of cities as it expanded. Chery, China’s largest exporter, came into existence after the city of Wuhu in the south-eastern province of Anhui sold a cement business and decided to launch a carmaker. AP The bottom-up model produced some of China’s most successful companies. But it also encouraged local officials to back as many contenders as possible, creating excess capacity. Even though the property downturn that began five years ago left regional governments with less revenue from land sales, they arguably now have an even greater incentive to develop industries that can replenish their coffers. This could explain why the number of automakers selling new-energy cars has not substantially declined, even as margins and profitability have fallen due to greater competition. Last year, 23 new brands entered the industry, while only nine exited. Consolidation may make economic sense, but it often runs counter to political incentives. Local governments remain reluctant to let hometown stalwarts fail because they provide potential job growth during an economic downturn. That’s an uncomfortable reality for Beijing and its trade partners.
